The kitchen was Rosa's own, with her twins asleep upstairs, not the fire academy's practice set, built for a training class. When the firefighters were done, the cabinet over the hob was ash and the staircase to the bedrooms was untouched. This was happening tonight, not a night from thirty years ago. Water dripped from the ceiling onto the tiles. Somewhere a radio was still playing, and the alarm kept up its thin, high whine.

When I turned the tin over, the cake came out whole and the paper lining stayed stuck to the bottom. This was this morning, not a morning fifteen years ago. Flour hung in the air. The radio by the sink played the same song it always played on Saturdays.

Lightning lit the windows of the arrivals hall, and the screen above the gate flickered as the storm hit the coast. On board flight 212 was Lena's son, flying alone for the first time, not a cargo of spare machine parts for a factory. The tracker showed that it had landed on the runway, not lost contact over the sea. Lena was watching the screen at this moment, not reading an old printout from twenty years ago. Rain hammered on the glass roof. A cleaner pushed a trolley past the empty seats, one wheel squeaking.

Outside, lorries idled in a long line, their engines rumbling.
